title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from §§10-12). Euler replaces the column by a discrete model: two rigid halves AC and CB, each of length a, joined at the midpoint C by an elastic hinge. The lower end B stands on the ground and the upper end A is held on the vertical line by a horizontal force. The hinge resists bending with a restoring moment 2Ee·θ when each half is tilted by the small angle θ, so the relative rotation is 2θ. M is the weight of each half, and a horizontal force C acts at the middle. Moment equilibrium of either half gave 2Eeθ = ½Ca + Maθ, hence θ = Ca/(4Ee − 2Ma) and C = (2θ/a)(2Ee − Ma).

This page opens by noting that C = 0 when Ma = 2Ee. Then a deflection with arbitrary θ needs no lateral force, so the column is in neutral equilibrium under its own weight and will collapse. This is the critical case Euler set out to treat.

§13 makes it concrete. Take total height b (so a = b/2), cross-section d², and unit specific weight, so M = ½d²b. The critical condition Ma = 2Ee becomes ¼b²d² = 2Ee, giving b = √(8Ee/d²). Any such column (flexible only at its middle, with resisting moment Ee) of this height or more cannot carry its own weight and falls flat.

Euler presents this explicitly as a new argument against his own earlier opinion that no column can fail under its own weight; that opinion is the paradox of the preceding paper on columns (E509, per my recollection of the Eneström sequence). Here a simple model with a finite critical height refutes the earlier analysis.

§14 starts the continuous problem. The lateral test force C is spread uniformly, C dx/b per element, so the column bends into a continuous curve. The self-weight load per element (M dx/b, with M now the whole weight) follows on the next page.

Modern reading: this is a rigid-link/rotational-spring (single-degree-of-freedom) stability model for buckling under self-weight. Energy check: the spring stores 2Eeθ². Gravity releases M(aθ²/4) from the lower half and M(3aθ²/4) from the upper half, total Maθ². Stability is lost at Ma = 2Ee, exactly as Euler finds.
errors: None in the mathematics. The critical condition Ma = 2Ee agrees with an independent energy calculation for the two-bar spring model, and M = ½d²b with a = b/2 does give ¼b²d² = 2Ee, so b = √(8Ee/d²).
Implicit assumption: unit specific weight, so weight equals volume d²b; this is unstated.
The constant Ee of the lumped hinge is not identified with the continuous stiffness Ekk used later. The numerical height is therefore only qualitative.

ideas.what: Neutral equilibrium / critical load found as the condition under which zero lateral force sustains an arbitrary small deflection (C = 0 for any θ)
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum I; E238; column papers E508-E511

ideas.what: Discrete two-rigid-bar model with an elastic hinge at mid-height buckling under self-weight; critical height b = √(8Ee/d²)
ideas.modern_name: rigid-link / rotational-spring stability model (Shanley-type idealization), self-weight buckling
ideas.usually_credited_to: textbook idealization (20th-century stability texts); self-weight buckling of the continuous column usually credited to Greenhill (1881)
ideas.where_published: this paper E510 (Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 1778); discussed by Truesdell in the Opera omnia II.11 commentary (unsure of exact pages)

ideas.what: Using a test lateral load distributed uniformly along the column to probe the continuous problem
ideas.modern_name: perturbation by a uniformly distributed lateral load / imperfection approach to stability

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds an early, clean discrete (rigid bar + rotational spring) buckling model used to refute Euler's own earlier no-collapse paradox. That is historically interesting, but the E509-E511 sequence and Euler's self-correction are covered in Truesdell's history of elasticity. The computation is elementary and correct.
transcription_corrections: Line 1: the image reads 'euoluere' with a smudged ending; the transcription 'euoluere' is correct.
The transcription is otherwise faithful: 'a = ½b', 'M = ½ddb', '¼bbdd = 2Ee' and 'b = √(8Ee/dd)' all match the image.
